vignette:
Margaret's Careful Calculations

Margaret sits in the leather chair across from the therapist's desk, her posture impeccably straight despite her seventy-one years. Her silver hair is arranged neatly, and her hands rest in her lap, fingers interlaced so tightly her knuckles blanch white. She is meticulous in appearance-pressed blouse, coordinated jewelry, nails filed to precise rectangles. This precision extends to everything she does. It always has.

Forty-three years ago, Margaret was working as a junior analyst at a banking firm in Phnom Penh. She was twenty-eight, newly married, and believed she had built a secure life through her intelligence and discipline. In 1981, she was at the office when armed soldiers entered the building. They took her and three colleagues to a detention facility on the outskirts of the city. She was held for eleven months.

She doesn't speak about those months in linear detail. Instead, the memories surface in fragments-the smell of the cell, the sound of footsteps in the corridor that made her stomach contract with terror, the way she counted the bars on the window obsessively as a way to maintain her mind. She was interrogated repeatedly about her family's finances, about foreign contacts, about her education abroad. She learned quickly to say nothing, to become small and invisible.

When she was finally released through a negotiated exchange, she weighed ninety-two pounds. Her husband had remarried. She had no family left in Cambodia.

Margaret emigrated to the United States and rebuilt herself. She obtained her American credentials, worked her way up to senior analyst at a respected firm, and maintained the same precision that had kept her alive in captivity-meticulous planning, control over every variable, an almost compulsive attention to detail. For decades, this worked. She was successful, respected, and outwardly composed.

But the control has become increasingly fragile.

Now, in her early seventies and recently retired, Margaret finds herself unable to sleep. Not occasionally-nearly every night, she lies awake until 3 or 4 a.m., her mind cycling through worst-case scenarios. She has begun checking her apartment locks multiple times before bed, sometimes returning to verify them again at 2 a.m. She knows this is excessive. She knows her locked apartment in a secure building is safe. But knowing and feeling are different things.

Certain sounds-a door slamming, an unexpected knock, raised voices in the hallway-send her heart into a panicked gallop. She finds herself holding her breath. Her hands shake. She has stopped attending the book club she joined after retirement because the restaurant where they meet has only one exit, and this detail fills her with dread she cannot quite explain.

The loss of her work structure has been destabilizing. For forty years, the job provided purpose and scaffolding-spreadsheets, meetings, clear objectives. Numbers don't betray. Data doesn't imprison. But retirement means time, and time means her mind wanders to places she has spent decades avoiding. She finds herself researching the fates of others detained during that period, reading historical accounts, watching documentaries. She knows this isn't helpful, yet she cannot stop.

Her daughter-born after her release, the one bright thing she built-has gently suggested therapy. Margaret resisted for years. She survived. She succeeded. What good would talking do? But the nightmares have intensified. Last month, she woke gasping, convinced she was back in the cell, and it took her twenty minutes to orient herself to reality.

She is here now, sitting across from this therapist, trying to find the words for why a woman with a successful career and a comfortable retirement suddenly feels like she is unraveling.
